meta.regime: Two independent regime-level events landed across the weekend and they push the same way: the Federal Reserve turned hawkish and the war restarted. Warsh used his first Jackson Hole keynote to say inflation trends have not meaningfully improved, that the labour market is effectively at full employment and that financial conditions are not restraining the economy, which repriced September from roughly a coin-flip-minus to 57-60% and took the dollar to a two-week high; at the same time US and Iranian forces exchanged fire for the first time since July 29, lifting WTI 3.87% and European gas to its highest since January 2023. The result is a board where six of eight currencies now have a live tightening story and the two that do not - sterling and the franc - become the funding legs. The single most informative price remains gold, which fell through 4,450 on an actual missile exchange: the haven complex is trading real rates, not the Strait.
meta.nextBigEvent: US August non-farm payrolls, Friday September 4 at 12:30Z. Warsh has explicitly removed the labour market as an objection by calling it full employment; July printed MINUS 23,000. A second negative payroll is the one thing that can unwind the entire hawkish repricing before the September 16 FOMC. Euro-area flash HICP tomorrow at 09:00Z and the RBNZ/BoC double on Wednesday come first.

dailyRead: Friday's file said the whole dollar score was deferred to one event and that broad dollar legs should be kept small until Warsh had spoken. He spoke, and he was hawkish, so the deferral resolves and the dollar is upgraded two notches from minus 1 to plus 1. The substance matters more than the tone: Warsh said recent reports do not tell him that underlying trends have meaningfully improved, cited PCE running at 3.7% over the past year and 4.1% annualised over the past six months, described the labour market as effectively at full employment, and said financial conditions may not be restraining the economy at all - then closed with the line that the Fed will have work to do if it does not get the confidence it needs. That last clause is what repriced the curve. September hike odds moved from roughly 30% on Thursday to 57-60% across CME futures and prediction markets, the 2-year Treasury went from 4.22% to 4.30%, and the dollar sits at a two-week high with DXY 99.511. Read the second sentence honestly, though: 57% is not a done deal, and Warsh himself made the August CPI report that lands days before the September 16 meeting the decisive input. The reason this is an upgrade to plus 1 and not plus 2 is that the labour market has not actually improved - July was MINUS 23,000 with unemployment at 4.1% - and Friday's payroll is the single event that can take the whole repricing back. The second event is that the war restarted. US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island that were, according to Washington, preparing to deploy sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz; the IRGC retaliated with ballistic missiles against the US-operated King Hussein and Al Azraq air bases in Jordan, eight of which Jordan says it intercepted, and against an air base in the UAE. It is the first exchange of fire since July 29 and it ends a month-long pause after a week of failed mediation. Tehran additionally reports that a supertanker on the southern Hormuz route struck two mines, which is unconfirmed. Energy repriced hard: WTI is 86.63 and up 3.87% on the day, Brent 91.12, European TTF gas 69.97 EUR/MWh and up 4.47% to its highest level since January 2023 with storage only 63% full in the final week of August, UK gas 164.82 GBp/therm and up 11.18% on the month, coal up 6.27% on the week. Traders now estimate only 6-8 million barrels a day still transiting the Strait, mostly from non-Iranian Gulf producers. Canada is the clearest beneficiary and is upgraded from zero to plus 1 on two separate legs. The oil leg is obvious. The growth leg is better than anyone expected: Q2 GDP printed plus 3.3% annualised, the fastest since early 2023 and comfortably above the Bank of Canada's own 2.5% call, and critically Statistics Canada REVISED the Q1 contraction away, restating it at plus 0.3% annualised, which removes the recession from the record entirely. The composition also answers Friday's objection directly. This was not a pure net-export bounce: exports rose 3.6% on a rebound in passenger cars and light trucks, but household spending rose too and business capital investment was up 2.3%, ending five consecutive quarters of decline. TE now carries quarterly growth at 0.8% from 0.1% and annual growth at 1.1% from 0.1%, with core CPI up to 2.3% from 2.1% and headline at 3.0%. What keeps the loonie at plus 1 rather than higher is unchanged and still real - the C$27.6bn retaliation on roughly 700 US product lines begins on September 8, services are at 49.1 and retail sales at minus 0.8% - and the Bank of Canada decides on Wednesday at 13:45Z, where a hold with heavy tariff language is the risk to this score. Sterling is the day's downgrade, from plus 1 to zero. Nothing broke in the UK data; what changed is the rest of the board. GBP was always a carry score rather than a policy score, and that carry now sits against a Fed pricing 57% for a hike, an ECB at 80% for September 10, a BoJ at 87% for September 18 and an RBNZ hiking on Wednesday - while UK rate-hike expectations are being reduced further, with markets looking past September 17 to November at the earliest. The domestic data supports the downgrade rather than resisting it: core CPI FLAT at 2.6% for a third month, services cooling, wage growth down to 4.1% from 4.4%, retail sales minus 0.5% and employment change halved to plus 83,000. Cable at 1.35436 is little changed on the day but has given up ground since Friday. The euro holds plus 2 and remains the strongest currency on this board, with the best single data point of the weekend behind it: Spain's flash August CPI came in at 4.3%, up SEVEN tenths from 3.6% and driven by fuel, with Spanish core easing a tenth to 2.9%. Euro-area energy inflation was already running at 10.3% in July and the gas move since then has been violently in one direction, so tomorrow's area-wide flash HICP at 09:00Z is the last inflation input before September 10 and the risk is skewed upward. Traders price roughly 80% for a hike to a 2.50% deposit rate next week with a further 40% by December. The honest counterweight is unchanged from Friday: the July accounts stressed avoiding pre-commitment, and a gas shock is a terms-of-trade hit to the euro area as well as an inflation impulse - which is precisely why the DAX fell 0.61% today, ending a four-day run to record highs with Siemens Energy down more than 4%. Japan holds plus 1 but the tape has gone against it. USD/JPY traded up to 160.071 on Sunday, breaching the level that both Tokyo and Washington have treated as a political line since the July 31 joint intervention, and sits at 159.636 now, down 0.26% on the day. The policy case is stronger than ever - BoJ September pricing is now around 87%, up from 80% on Friday and from 23% before the July meeting, with Tokyo core CPI at a five-month high of 1.8%, core-core at 2.0%, the jobless rate at a one-year low of 2.4% and retail sales up 4.0% y/y - but the pair went through 160 anyway, which tells you how much the Warsh repricing is worth. USD/JPY stays a short because the BoJ is better priced than the Fed and the official sector is on the same side, but it comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM: the dollar leg has flipped against the trade and a sustained hold above 160 without an MoF response is the invalidation. Australia holds plus 1 on an unchanged monetary leg - trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% annual with the monthly at plus 0.5%, the G10's highest cash rate at 4.35%, consumer confidence recovering to 88.9 from 83.9 - but the industrial leg has quietly weakened, and this matters. Copper has now fallen for four straight sessions on a stronger dollar, the spot-over-three-month premium has narrowed and LME inventories have improved as deliveries increased, which is the first real evidence that the physical squeeze behind the copper long is easing. Q2 GDP lands Wednesday at 01:30Z with a TE forecast of 0.0% q/q against a labour market that shed 15,827 jobs in July. New Zealand holds plus 1 into the nearest and best-evidenced event on the calendar: the RBNZ is expected to hike to 2.75% on Wednesday at 02:00Z, ASB and Westpac both call it, consensus among all six committee members is likely, and it is close to fully priced - so the OCR track, expected to imply 3.0% by year-end with a peak near 3.3%, matters far more than the decision. Switzerland stays at zero and the reasoning is now three tests deep. The franc has failed to bid on a de-escalation headline, on a re-escalation headline, and now on an actual exchange of ballistic missiles: USD/CHF ROSE to 0.80819 and EUR/CHF is still pinned around 0.9376. That is not a weak haven, it is an absent one. The reason CHF does not go to minus 1 today is that the Swiss real economy is improving underneath - the services PMI jumped to 63.9 from 59.8 and business confidence to 107 - and Swiss CPI lands tomorrow at 06:30Z with a TE forecast of 0.7% against 0.4% now. Four score changes in one session is a lot, and the discipline for the rest of this week is to let the CHF question resolve on data rather than add a fifth. The practical book: EUR/GBP is now the only two-notch gap on the board and is the cleanest trade here; USD/CHF and CAD/CHF are the clean expressions of the new dollar and the new loonie against the funding franc; sell sterling against the kiwi and the yen; keep USOIL long but sized for the fact that this complex has whipsawed three times in a week; and be short gold, which just told you exactly what it is trading.

USD.when: Sept 16, 18:00Z - UPGRADED from hold: futures and prediction markets now price 57-60% for +25bp to 4.00%
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning and the hard data is unchanged - policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% with core 2.5%, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000, GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1% - but the reaction function changed completely on Friday. Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole keynote to say that recent reports do not tell him underlying inflation trends have meaningfully improved, that PCE is running 3.7% over the past year and 4.1% annualised over six months, that the labour market is effectively at full employment, and that financial conditions may not be restraining the economy at all, before saying the Fed will have work to do absent the confidence it needs. September odds went from roughly 30% on Thursday to 57-60% across CME futures and prediction markets, the 2-year moved 4.22% to 4.30%, and the dollar is at a two-week high with DXY 99.511. This is why USD is upgraded two notches from -1 to +1: Friday's file explicitly deferred the score to this event, and the event resolved hawkish. Be precise about the limits. 57% is not a done deal, Warsh made the August CPI report landing days before the meeting the decisive input, and the labour market has not improved - which makes Friday's payroll at 12:30Z the single largest risk to the whole repricing. Supporting evidence unchanged: the July 29 decision was a 9-3 hold with all three dissents FOR a hike, four regional Reserve Banks sought a discount-rate increase, and Collins said on Aug 25 that tightening soon will be appropriate. Today's TE data also shows consumer confidence falling to 51.7 from 55.2 and retail sales -0.6%, which is the counterargument nobody is pricing.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z - roughly 80% priced for +25bp to a 2.50% deposit rate, with a further 40% by December
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike; main refinancing 2.40%. Use 2.25%. EUR holds +2 and remains the strongest currency on the board. The weekend delivered the best single print available to the hawks: Spain's flash August CPI at 4.3%, up SEVEN tenths from 3.6% in July, driven by fuel and lubricants for private vehicles rising where they fell a year earlier, with Spanish core easing only a tenth to 2.9%. Euro-area energy inflation was already accelerating to 10.3% from 8.5% in the July release as hostilities resumed, and the gas move since has been one-way - TTF 69.97 EUR/MWh and up 4.47% today to its highest since January 2023, with storage 63% full in the final week of August and Gulf LNG still disrupted. TE macro re-verified: HICP 2.9% with core 2.5%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, unemployment 6.3%, manufacturing PMI 52.8 at a four-year high, services 51.7, wage growth 3.4% from 3.1%, producer price change decelerating to 4.6% from 5.9%. The July accounts remain the policy anchor: the pause was NOT the end of the tightening cycle, another hike is likely unless the outlook improves significantly, and some members would not have opposed a July move. The honest caveats: those same accounts stressed avoiding pre-commitment and keeping September open, and a gas shock is a terms-of-trade hit as well as an inflation impulse - visible today in the DAX falling 0.61% off record highs with Siemens Energy down more than 4%. Area-wide flash HICP tomorrow at 09:00Z is the last input before the decision.

GBP.when: Sept 17, 11:00Z - and hike expectations are being pushed further out, to November at the earliest
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%, held 6-3 on Jul 30 with three voting for 4.00%. GBP is DOWNGRADED from +1 to 0, and the reason is comparative rather than domestic. Sterling has always been a carry score here, resting on a 10-year gilt near 4.99%, the highest in the G10. That carry is now measured against a Fed pricing 57% for September, an ECB at 80% for September 10, a BoJ at 87% for September 18 and an RBNZ hiking on Wednesday - while UK rate-hike expectations are explicitly being reduced further. When every comparator repriced hawkish in one weekend and sterling did not, a relative score has to move. The domestic data supports it rather than resisting it: TE re-verified CPI 2.9% but core FLAT at 2.6% for a third month, wage growth DOWN to 4.1% from 4.4%, employment change halved to +83k, retail sales -0.5% m/m, GDP +0.4% q/q from +0.6%. The one genuine offset is energy - UK gas at 164.82 GBp/therm and up 11.18% on the month keeps the Ofgem channel that produced July's print open into the next cap window, and consumer confidence improved to -14 from -17. There is no UK data of consequence before September 17, which means sterling will trade as the funding leg of other currencies stories all week. Sell it against the kiwi, the yen, the Aussie and the loonie; buy the euro against it - EUR/GBP is now the only two-notch gap on this board.

JPY.when: Sept 18, 03:00Z - now roughly 87% priced for +25bp to 1.25%, up from 80% on Friday and 23% before the July meeting
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, the highest since September 1995, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY holds +1 and the policy case is the strongest it has been all year, but the tape went the other way and that has to be said plainly. USD/JPY traded up to 160.071 on Sunday, breaching the level that both Tokyo and Washington have treated as a political line in the sand since the first joint intervention since 1998 on July 31, and now sits at 159.636, down 0.26% on the day. Breaching 160 on the same weekend the Fed turned hawkish is a measure of how much the Warsh repricing is worth against an 87%-priced BoJ hike. The data is unambiguous: TE re-verified Tokyo core CPI 1.8% against 1.7% expected, a five-month high and a third straight acceleration, Tokyo CPI ex food and energy at 2.0% from 1.8%, national CPI 1.9% with core 1.8%, the jobless rate at 2.4% and a one-year low, jobs-to-applications 1.18, wage growth 3.4%, manufacturing PMI 55.1, services 52.3, and retail sales +2.4% m/m and +4.0% y/y. Annual GDP growth was revised up to 0.7% from 0.5%. Deputy Governor Himino has publicly urged timely hikes. The trade therefore stays short USD/JPY - the BoJ is better priced than the Fed and the official sector sits on the same side - but conviction comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM, because the dollar leg has flipped from a tailwind to a headwind. A sustained hold above 160 without an MoF response is the invalidation, not a level to add into. The structural offset also worsened: crude at 86.63 reopens the import-price drag that has capped the yen all year.

AUD.when: Sept 29, 04:30Z - odds around 27%, the lowest hike probability of any tightening bank on this board
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, the G10's highest, held Aug 11. AUD holds +1 but the composition of that score has changed and the change is not favourable. The monetary leg is intact: the July CPI indicator left the RBA's preferred trimmed mean UNCHANGED at 3.6% annual, its highest since September 2024, with the monthly at +0.5% against 0.3% expected and breadth in market goods and services excluding volatiles at +1.0% m/m - a domestic, demand-side inflation case that does not depend on which way the Strait goes, which is exactly why the Aussie has survived every geopolitical whipsaw of the past week unchanged. TE also re-verified headline 3.5%, consumer confidence recovering to 88.9 from 83.9, manufacturing PMI 52.0 and services 52.9. The industrial leg is what weakened. Copper is 6.6039 USD/lb but has now fallen for FOUR straight sessions as the dollar strengthened, the premium for spot over three-month futures has narrowed, and LME inventories have improved as deliveries increased - the first real evidence that the physical squeeze underpinning the copper long is easing. That removes the second independent leg the Aussie was carrying. What still caps it at +1 is the labour market: July employment FELL 15,827, unemployment 4.5% at a post-COVID high, wage growth 3.2%. Q2 GDP on Wednesday at 01:30Z carries a TE forecast of 0.0% q/q with annual growth 2.5%; TE has also revised the prior quarter to 0.3% from 0.9%.

NZD.when: Sept 2, 02:00Z - +25bp to 2.75% is close to fully priced, with consensus likely across all six committee members
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.50% after the Jul 8 hike, the first in three years, taken on a 3-3 split with Governor Breman casting the deciding vote. NZD holds +1 into the nearest event on the board. ASB and Westpac both call a 25bp move to 2.75% on Wednesday, the shadow board mostly backs it, and unlike July the decision is expected to be reached by consensus among all six voters rather than a casting vote. Because the decision itself is close to fully priced, the OCR TRACK is what trades: ASB expects the projection to signal at least one further 25bp hike by year end with a published peak near 3.3%, and the Bank's own projections are likely to imply 3.0% by December. A track at or above that is a kiwi bid; a track that stops at 2.75% takes the score straight back to zero. catalysts.note: July was 0.4% and a four-month low with the first monthly fall in six; TE forecasts 0.7% for August. This is the print that decides whether CHF stays at zero or gets downgraded to -1 - a soft number confirms the pure funding-currency read and strengthens every short-franc cross on the board.

The aggregate after Spain printed 4.3%, up SEVEN tenths from 3.6% on fuel. July was 2.9% with core 2.5% and energy inflation already accelerating to 10.3%; TTF gas has since risen to its highest since January 2023. The last inflation input before Sept 10 and the only number that could still talk the Governing Council out of a move.

The first hard US read after Warsh, and a test of whether Q2's resilient consumption carried into Q3. TE has manufacturing PMI at 53.2 from 53.9, with consumer confidence having fallen to 51.7 from 55.2 and retail sales at -0.6%.

TE forecast 0.0% q/q with annual growth 2.5%; the prior quarter has been revised to 0.3% from 0.9%. The soft counterweight to the trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% - a flat print complicates the Sept 29 hike case and is the main risk to AUD at +1.

catalysts.event: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement and OCR decision
catalysts.note: +25bp to 2.75% is close to fully priced, with ASB and Westpac both calling it and consensus likely across all six voters rather than July's casting vote. Because the decision is priced, the OCR TRACK is the trade: ASB expects a peak near 3.3% and the Bank's own projections likely imply 3.0% by December. A track stopping at 2.75% takes NZD back to zero.

A seventh straight hold at 2.25% is consensus, six days before the C$27.6bn retaliatory tariffs take effect. After a +3.3% annualised Q2 and the Q1 contraction being revised away, watch whether the statement leans on that strength or on tariff risk - heavy tariff language is the specific thing that returns CAD to zero.

catalysts.event: US August employment report / non-farm payrolls
catalysts.note: THE event of the week and the largest single risk on this board. July printed MINUS 23,000 with unemployment at 4.1% and average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m. Warsh has explicitly removed the labour market as an objection by calling it full employment - a second negative payroll contradicts him directly and can unwind the entire 57-60% September repricing before the FOMC.

C$27.6bn (about US$19.9bn) across roughly 700 US product lines at 15%, 25% and 50% - steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics - matching US 50% duties on about US$20bn of Canadian goods, alongside a C$7.5bn domestic support package. The hard cap on any further CAD upgrade.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision + Lagarde press conference
catalysts.note: Roughly 80% priced for +25bp to a 2.50% deposit rate, with a further 40% priced by December. The July accounts say the pause was not the end of the cycle, and Spain's 4.3% flash print plus gas at a January-2023 high both harden the case. The biggest scheduled event for the strongest currency on the board. Presser 12:45Z.

Warsh singled this out as the decisive input: the price report landing days before the September meeting will play an outsize role in whether the Fed acts. July was 3.4% headline with core 2.5%, and PCE is running 3.7% y/y and 4.1% annualised over six months. Verify the exact release date against the BLS calendar before positioning.

Now a genuine live meeting: 57-60% priced for +25bp to a 4.00% upper bound after Warsh said the Fed will have work to do. July was a 9-3 hold with all three dissents FOR a hike, and four regional Reserve Banks separately sought a discount-rate increase.

Hold expected at 3.75% after the 6-3 July split with three voting for 4.00%, and hike expectations are now being pushed out to November at the earliest - which is why GBP was downgraded to zero. UK gas +11.18% on the month is the one thing that could convert the dissenters.

Roughly 87% priced for +25bp to 1.25%, up from 80% on Friday and just 23% before the July meeting, which would be the highest policy rate since 1995. Tokyo core CPI at a five-month high, Tokyo core-core at 2.0%, the jobless rate at a one-year low and Himino urging timely hikes all point the same way.

A Reuters poll unanimously expects zero, held through 2026. Watch the intervention language rather than the rate - Schlegel has repeated his readiness to act against rapid franc appreciation, though after three failed haven tests the franc is nowhere near needing it.

Hike odds around 27%, the lowest of any tightening bank on this board, with the trimmed mean stuck at 3.6%. The August minutes show the Board weighed a pre-emptive hike and did not discuss a cut; Hauser said the Bank will need to raise again if upside risks materialise.

Live and kinetic again after a month-long pause. US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island preparing to deploy sea mines into the Strait; the IRGC fired ballistic missiles at the US-operated King Hussein and Al Azraq air bases in Jordan, eight of which Jordan intercepted, and at a UAE air base; Tehran reports a supertanker struck two mines on the southern route, unconfirmed. A week of mediation failed. Traders estimate only 6-8 mb/d still transiting. Every CAD, NZD, CHF, XAU, GER40 and USOIL position here is a partial bet on which way this goes, and it has whipsawed three times in a week.

ESCALATED. USD/JPY printed 160.071 on Sunday, breaching the level Washington and Tokyo turned into a political line after the first joint intervention since 1998 on July 31, when a 40-year high of 163.73 was met with coordinated yen-buying that took the pair to 155-156. The pair has now retraced the entire move with no follow-up action. The standard MoF sequence into this level is jawboning, then rate-checking, then acting - but the breach without a response is also why USD/JPY comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM today.

geopolitics: The war restarted this weekend and it is the first genuine kinetic escalation in a month. US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island after the IRGC was observed preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz; Iran retaliated with ballistic missiles against the US-operated King Hussein and Al Azraq air bases in Jordan, eight of which Jordan's military says it intercepted in its airspace early on August 31, and against US forces and helicopters at an air base in the UAE. It is the first exchange of fire since July 29 and it follows a week in which mediation failed to break the stalemate. Tehran additionally reports that a supertanker attempting the southern Hormuz route struck two mines, which has not been independently confirmed. Energy repriced immediately and hard: WTI is 86.63 and up 3.87% on the day, Brent 91.12 and up 3.43%, European TTF gas 69.97 EUR/MWh and up 4.47% to its highest level since January 2023 with EU storage only 63% full in the final week of August and Gulf LNG still disrupted, UK gas 164.82 GBp/therm and up 11.18% on the month, and coal up 6.27% on the week. Traders now estimate that only 6-8 million barrels a day still transit the Strait, mainly from non-Iranian Gulf producers, against Washington's continuing naval blockade and economic pressure campaign. Keep two counterweights in view. Crude is up only about 2% across August as a whole after a 22% surge in July, so the underlying trend is far less one-directional than a single 3.87% session suggests, and this complex has now reversed three times inside a week. The FX transmission is cleaner than the geopolitics. Canada is the direct beneficiary and, combined with a Q2 GDP beat and the Q1 recession being revised away, is upgraded to +1. The euro is reinforced at +2 because gas at a January-2023 high is exactly the inflation channel the ECB keeps citing, and Spain's 4.3% flash CPI is that channel showing up in the data - though the same shock is a euro-area terms-of-trade hit, which is why the DAX fell 0.61% off record highs with industrials leading and Siemens Energy down more than 4%. New Zealand's +1 rests partly on this too, since the RBNZ's July MPS named a partial reopening of Hormuz as the reason headline inflation would fall back toward 2%, and that assumption is now dead. But the single most important observation is again a negative one, and it is now three tests deep: gold fell THROUGH 4,450 and the Swiss franc WEAKENED to 0.80819 on a day when American and Iranian forces exchanged ballistic missiles. The haven complex is not pricing the Strait at all. It is pricing US real rates and a 57-60% September Fed hike, which is why Warsh's keynote outranks every headline out of the Gulf on this board, and why XAU flips from RANGE to SHORT while the franc stays a funding currency.
